niche.intro: The niches below are listed because they work for Filipino online professionals right now, as of 2026. But "right now" always changes. New niches emerge, old ones saturate, AI reshapes what pays. The list below will eventually go stale. The rubric that produced it won't.
niche.creed: A list of niches is a snapshot. The ability to evaluate any niche is permanent.
niche.examplesNote: The niches below are worked examples of this rubric, already scored against real 2026 demand. Study *why* each one lands where it does, then run the same seven questions on a niche we never listed. That's the actual skill.

criteria.name: Real demand
criteria.question: Are there live job posts for this, this week?
criteria.why: A niche can look perfect on paper and still have nobody hiring for it. Demand overrides every other good answer, no live openings means no clients, no matter how much you'd enjoy the work.

criteria.name: Pay ceiling
criteria.question: What do the top people in this niche earn?
criteria.why: Starting pay tells you what's true today. The ceiling tells you if it's worth three years of your life, some niches top out fast, others keep paying more the longer you're in them.

criteria.name: Barrier to entry
criteria.question: Can I be credible to a client in 90 days?
criteria.why: A niche you can't credibly enter for a year isn't wrong, it just isn't your first niche. You need income while you're still learning, so pick something you can prove within a season.

criteria.name: Competition
criteria.question: How many other people can do this as well as I can?
criteria.why: If ten thousand people can do exactly what you do, clients pick on price, and price wars favor whoever's desperate, not whoever's good. Low competition, or a real way to stand out, protects your rate.

criteria.name: Fit
criteria.question: Would I still choose this on a bad day?
criteria.why: Pay and demand get you hired. Fit gets you to year two. The niches that burn people out are usually the ones picked for the pay band alone, not because the daily work suited them.

criteria.name: Durability
criteria.question: Is AI or automation eating this job in the next 3 years?
criteria.why: Some niches are one task an AI model can already do in a single prompt, those are shrinking fast. Others need judgment, relationships, or representing a business, which stay harder to automate. Bet on the second kind.

criteria.name: Transferability
criteria.question: Do these skills carry to a better role or niche later?
criteria.why: If this niche doesn't work out, or you outgrow it, do the skills open other doors? A niche that teaches you nothing transferable is a dead end even while it's still paying well.

howToResearch.title: Run a live job-post audit
howToResearch.desc: Search Indeed, OnlineJobs.ph, Upwork, and LinkedIn for the niche's actual job title. Filter to posted this week. If nothing is live right now, the niche isn't in demand today, whatever anyone else claims.

howToResearch.title: Read 20 real listings, not 2
howToResearch.desc: Two listings show you nothing, twenty show you the pattern: the tools every client mentions, the years of experience they ask for, the tasks that repeat. That pattern is the real job description. Write it down.

howToResearch.title: Study 5 senior profiles
howToResearch.desc: Find 5 people already doing this niche for 2+ years, on LinkedIn, Upwork, or a Facebook group. What do they charge now versus when they started? What did they add along the way to get there? That's your real pay ceiling and your roadmap.

howToResearch.title: Stress-test it against AI
howToResearch.desc: Search "[niche] AI replace" and deliberately read sources that disagree with each other, not three that agree with you. If the job is "do a task a model can now do in one prompt," the ceiling is falling. If it's "judge, decide, or represent a business," it holds up longer.

howToResearch.title: Run the bad-day test on yourself
howToResearch.desc: Picture your worst week: an annoying client, low energy, still three hours of work left. Would you still rather be doing this than any other niche on your shortlist? If the honest answer is no, fit is broken, no matter how good the pay band looks on paper.

equipment.intro: The useful skill is knowing which specs and failure points to test. Check the requirements for the tools you use before you compare prices.
equipment.referenceNote: Three example builds to measure your own list against.

whatMatters.spec: RAM and storage, before CPU badges
whatMatters.whatMattersAndWhy: RAM headroom helps when several tabs, apps, and a call are open together. An SSD usually makes booting and opening files quicker than a mechanical hard drive. Results still depend on your workload, so a processor label alone cannot tell you whether a laptop will feel fast enough.
whatMatters.howToJudge: Start with the published requirements for your heaviest app. As one reference, Adobe Photoshop lists 8GB RAM as its minimum and 16GB or more as recommended. Confirm the machine has an SSD, then test a workload that resembles your real shift.
whatMatters.dontOverpayFor: A newer processor badge by itself. Compare the complete machine: RAM, storage, battery condition, ports, warranty, and how it handles the apps you need.

whatMatters.spec: Upload capacity and stability, not only download speed
whatMatters.whatMattersAndWhy: Video calls and file uploads use upstream capacity, while the headline on a home plan usually describes download speed. Wi-Fi coverage, congestion, and other people on the connection can matter as much as the advertised plan speed.
whatMatters.howToJudge: Check the requirements for your calling app. Zoom's Web App currently recommends 3.8 Mbps upload and 3.0 Mbps download for 1080p group video, with lower requirements for 720p. Leave headroom for other devices and test at the hours you expect to work.
whatMatters.dontOverpayFor: More download speed before checking upload performance, peak-hour drops, router placement, and household sharing. Fix the bottleneck you can measure.

whatMatters.spec: A power backup, before a better webcam
whatMatters.whatMattersAndWhy: A short outage can end a call or erase unsaved work. The right backup depends on what must stay powered and how long you need to save, send a message, or switch connections.
whatMatters.howToJudge: Do not infer runtime from a 650VA label alone. List the wattage of every device you will connect, choose a target runtime, and use the manufacturer's load-specific runtime chart. Test the setup after buying it.
whatMatters.dontOverpayFor: Camera gear before you have backup power that matches your actual outage risk and device load.

whatMatters.spec: A noise-cancelling microphone, before a better camera
whatMatters.whatMattersAndWhy: Bad audio makes a call hard to follow even when the camera is adequate. Microphone placement, the room, and the noise around you all affect whether speech stays clear.
whatMatters.howToJudge: Test the headset in the room where you will work. Record a voice memo while the fan is running and while normal household noise is present; listen for clear speech, rubbing cables, hum, and sudden volume changes.
whatMatters.dontOverpayFor: Higher camera resolution before fixing audio, lighting, and framing that you already know are causing trouble.

whatMatters.spec: Battery health, not just the specs sheet, for anything secondhand
whatMatters.whatMattersAndWhy: A used laptop's RAM, processor, and storage do not show how much charge its battery still holds or whether its ports work reliably. Wear varies by unit, even between two machines with the same model number.
whatMatters.howToJudge: Ask for a battery report showing full-charge capacity beside design capacity, then test unplugged runtime with a normal workload. On Windows 11, Microsoft documents the built-in battery report. Also check the charger and every port you need.
whatMatters.dontOverpayFor: A "like new" description without a battery report, an unplugged test, and time to inspect the ports before payment.

source.label: Microsoft: caring for your battery in Windows

whatMatters.spec: A second monitor and ergonomic chair, real upgrades, wrong order
whatMatters.whatMattersAndWhy: A second screen can reduce window switching, and a chair that fits can make long sessions more comfortable. Neither item proves you can do the work, so treat both as later purchases unless your current setup is stopping you from working safely.
whatMatters.howToJudge: Ask yourself: would I lose a client or fail to apply without this? If no, it's a later purchase, once income is steady, not before you've landed your first client.
whatMatters.dontOverpayFor: A premium chair or monitor in month one. Adjust the setup you already own first, then upgrade when a measured work problem justifies the cost.

buyingSmart.title: Buy secondhand from the right places
buyingSmart.desc: Facebook Marketplace groups (search "laptop for sale [your city]"), Carousell, and local computer shops with a physical storefront and warranty are safer than a random online stranger. Meet in a public place with wifi so you can test the unit before paying, a mall, a coworking space, any Jollibee with wifi all work.

buyingSmart.title: Test before you pay, every time
buyingSmart.desc: Boot it up, open ten browser tabs plus a video call to check for lag, run a battery-health check, plug in the charger and wiggle the cable to check the port, and open a plain white window to check the screen for dead pixels or lines. Five minutes of testing saves you a ₱15,000 mistake.

buyingSmart.title: Red flags to walk away from
buyingSmart.desc: The seller won't let you test before paying. The price is far below every other listing for the same specs. They push GCash-only payment before you've seen the item in person. The serial number is scratched off or missing. Any one of these is a reason to walk, not negotiate.

buyingSmart.title: The rule that saves you money
buyingSmart.desc: Buy the cheapest thing that clears the bar for the work you're doing today. Don't buy for the job you hope to have in a year, you can always upgrade with your first month's pay. Overbuying upfront is money you can't use to survive the gap before your first client.
